{{Short description|Mathematical theory}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Alexander duality''' refers to a [[duality theory]] initiated by a result of [[James Waddell Alexander II|J. W. Alexander]] in 1915, and subsequently further developed, particularly by [[Pavel Alexandrov]] and [[Lev Pontryagin]]. It applies to the [[homology theory]] properties of the complement of a [[subspace topology|subspace]] ''X'' in [[Euclidean space]], a [[sphere]], or another [[manifold (mathematics)|manifold]]. It is generalized by [[Spanier–Whitehead duality]].

==General statement for spheres==
Let <math>X</math> be a non-empty [[compact space|compact]], [[locally contractible space|locally contractible]] subspace of the [[n-sphere|sphere]] <math>S^n</math> of dimension ''n''. Let <math>S^n\setminus X</math> be the complement of <math>X</math> in <math>S^n</math>. Then if <math>\tilde{H}</math> stands for [[reduced homology]] or [[reduced cohomology]], with coefficients in a given [[abelian group]], there is an [[isomorphism]]

:<math>\tilde{H}_q(S^n\setminus X) \cong \tilde{H}^{n-q-1}(X)</math>

for all <math>q\ge 0</math>.  Note that we can drop local contractibility as part of the hypothesis if we use reduced [[Čech cohomology]], which is designed to deal with local pathologies.

=== Applications ===
This is useful for computing the cohomology of [[Knot (mathematics)|knot]] and [[Link (knot theory)|link]] complements in <math>S^3</math>. Recall that a knot is an embedding <math>K\colon S^1 \hookrightarrow S^3</math> and a link is a disjoint union of knots, such as the [[Borromean rings]]. Then, if we write the link/knot as <math>L</math>, we have
:<math>\tilde{H}_q(S^3\setminus L) \cong \tilde{H}^{3-q-1}(L)</math>,
giving a method for computing the cohomology groups. In particular the dimension of the cohomology of the complement only depends on the homology of <math>L</math>, that is the number of its connected components (or number of strands). For example it is impossible to distinguish a borromean link from a trivial link (i.e. three separated circles). However it is possible to differentiate between different links using multiplicative operations on these cohomology spaces, like [[Cup product|cup-products]] and the [[Massey product]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Massey|first=William S.|author-link=William S. Massey|date=1998-05-01|title=Higher order linking numbers|url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0218216598000206|journal=[[Journal of Knot Theory and Its Ramifications]]|volume=7|issue=3|pages=393–414|doi=10.1142/S0218216598000206|issn=0218-2165|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210202191811/https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/surgery/uicc/massey.pdf|archive-date=2 Feb 2021|via=|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
For example, for the Borromean rings <math>L</math>, the homology groups are
:<math>\begin{align}
\tilde{H}_0(S^3 \setminus L)&\cong \tilde{H}^{2}(L) = 0 \\
\tilde{H}_1(S^3 \setminus L)&\cong \tilde{H}^{1}(L) = \Z^{\oplus 3}\\
\tilde{H}_2(S^3 \setminus L)&\cong \tilde{H}^{0}(L) = \Z^{\oplus 3}\\
\tilde{H}_3(S^3 \setminus L)&\cong 0 \\
\end{align}</math>

== Combinatorial Alexander duality ==
Let <math>X</math> be an [[abstract simplicial complex]] on a vertex set <math>V</math> of size <math>n</math>.
The Alexander dual <math>X^*</math> of <math>X</math> is defined as the simplicial complex on <math>V</math> whose faces are complements of non-faces of <math>X</math>. That is
: <math>X^* = \{ \sigma\ \colon\ V \setminus \sigma \not\in X\}</math>.
Note that <math>(X^*)^* = X</math>.

Alexander duality implies the following combinatorial analog (for [[reduced homology]] and [[reduced cohomology|cohomology]], with coefficients in any given [[abelian group]]):
:<math>\tilde{H}_q(X^*) \cong \tilde{H}^{n-q-3}(X)</math>
for all <math>q\ge 0</math>.
Indeed, this can be deduced by letting <math>Y \simeq S^{n-2}</math> be the [[N-skeleton|<math>(n-2)</math>-skeleton]] of the full simplex on <math>V</math> (that is, <math>Y</math> is the family of all subsets of size at most <math>n-1</math>) and showing that the [[Abstract simplicial complex#Geometric realization|geometric realization]] <math>|X^*|</math> is homotopy equivalent to <math>|Y| \setminus |X|</math>.
[[Anders Björner|Björner]] and Tancer presented an elementary combinatorial proof and summarized a few generalizations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Björner |first1=Anders |last2=Tancer |first2=Martin |title=Note: Combinatorial Alexander Duality—A Short and Elementary Proof |journal=Discrete & Computational Geometry |date=December 2009 |volume=42 |issue=4 |pages=586–593 |doi=10.1007/s00454-008-9102-x |arxiv=0710.1172}}</ref>

== Alexander duality for constructible sheaves ==
For [[smooth manifold]]s, Alexander duality is a formal consequence of [[Verdier duality]] for [[sheaf of abelian groups|sheaves of abelian groups]]. More precisely, if we let <math>X</math> denote a smooth manifold and we let <math>Y \subset X</math> be a closed subspace (such as a subspace representing a cycle, or a submanifold) represented by the inclusion <math>i\colon Y \hookrightarrow X</math>, and if <math>k</math> is a field, then if <math>\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Sh}_k(Y)</math> is a sheaf of <math>k</math>-vector spaces we have the following isomorphism<ref>{{Cite book|last=Iversen|first= Birger|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-82783-9
|title=Cohomology of sheaves|series= Universitext|date=1986|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer-Verlag]]|isbn=0-387-16389-1|location=Berlin|oclc=13269489}}</ref>{{rp|307}}
:<math>H^s_c(Y,\mathcal{F})^\vee \cong \operatorname{Ext}_k^{n-s}(i_*\mathcal{F}, \omega_X [n-s])</math>,
where the cohomology group on the left is [[Compactly-supported homology|compactly supported cohomology]]. We can unpack this statement further to get a better understanding of what it means. First, if <math>\mathcal{F} = \underline{k}</math> is the constant sheaf and <math>Y</math> is a smooth submanifold, then we get
:<math>\operatorname{Ext}_k^{n - s}(i_*\mathcal{F}, \omega_X [n-r]) \cong H^{n-s}_Y(X,\omega_X)</math>,
where the cohomology group on the right is [[local cohomology]] with support in <math>Y</math>. Through further reductions, it is possible to identify the homology of <math>X \setminus Y</math> with the cohomology of <math>Y</math>. This is useful in [[algebraic geometry]] for computing the cohomology groups of [[projective varieties]], and is exploited for constructing a basis of the [[Hodge structure]] of hypersurfaces of degree <math>d</math> using the [[Jacobian ideal|Jacobian ring]].

==Alexander's 1915 result== 
Referring to Alexander's original work, it is assumed that ''X'' is a [[simplicial complex]]. 

Alexander had little of the modern apparatus, and his result was only for the [[Betti number]]s, with coefficients taken ''modulo'' 2. What to expect comes from examples. For example the [[Clifford torus]] construction in the [[3-sphere]] shows that the complement of a [[solid torus]] is another solid torus; which will be open if the other is closed, but this does not affect its homology. Each of the solid tori is from the [[homotopy]] point of view a [[circle]]. If we just write down the Betti numbers

:1, 1, 0, 0

of the circle (up to <math>H_3</math>, since we are in the 3-sphere), then reverse as

:0, 0, 1, 1

and then shift one to the left to get

:0, 1, 1, 0

there is a difficulty, since we are not getting what we started with. On the other hand the same procedure applied to the ''reduced'' Betti numbers, for which the initial Betti number is decremented by 1, starts with

:0, 1, 0, 0

and gives

:0, 0, 1, 0

whence

:0, 1, 0, 0.

This ''does'' work out, predicting the complement's reduced Betti numbers.

The prototype here is the [[Jordan curve theorem]], which [[topology|topologically]] concerns the complement of a [[circle]] in the [[Riemann sphere]]. It also tells the same story. We have the honest Betti numbers

:1, 1, 0

of the circle, and therefore

:0, 1, 1

by flipping over and

:1, 1, 0

by shifting to the left. This gives back something different from what the Jordan theorem states, which is that there are two components, each [[contractible]] ([[Schoenflies theorem]], to be accurate about what is used here). That is, the correct answer in honest Betti numbers is 

:2, 0, 0.

Once more, it is the reduced Betti numbers that work out. With those, we begin with

:0, 1, 0

to finish with

:1, 0, 0.

From these two examples, therefore, Alexander's formulation can be inferred: reduced Betti numbers <math>\tilde{b}_i</math> are related in complements by

:<math>\tilde{b}_i \to \tilde{b}_{n-i-1}</math>.
